findings.evidence: Phrase: 'it accused an engineer of hiding a recorder in a toilet-paper roll'; alt: 'a person calmly sets down an ordinary toilet-paper roll' — this maps uniquely onto a real, named, currently-prosecuted individual (the BBC source names Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi OpenAI engineer arrested by the FBI), identifiable by the unique toilet-paper-roll recorder detail even though unnamed in the slopper text.
findings.suggestion: Drop the specific real criminal case, or rework the joke to focus on the institutional security lapse ('a recorder was found hidden in a toilet-paper roll at headquarters') rather than attributing the act to 'an engineer,' which combined with the unique prop maps directly onto one identifiable, currently-prosecuted person.

findings.evidence: Phrase 'it accused an engineer of hiding a recorder in a toilet-paper roll' vs. sources: the FBI arrested the engineer and charged him with foreign espionage ('FBI lobs foreign spy charges,' 'faces 5 years and $250K fine' — Ars Technica). The phrase reassigns the accusation from the FBI/federal prosecutors to the chatbot maker itself ('it accused'), and downgrades 'foreign spy charges' to a vague, lesser-sounding 'hiding a recorder.'
findings.suggestion: Attribute the accusation correctly, e.g. 'the FBI arrested an engineer there on spying charges after a recorder was found hidden in a toilet-paper roll,' so the actor (FBI, not the company) and the severity (criminal espionage charge, not just 'hiding a recorder') match the sources.
